arguments.argument: The entire debate assumes AI-generated prototype code must become the production codebase — but the highest-leverage move is to treat the AI prototype as a disposable specification artifact: a fast, cheap way to validate the hypothesis that gets deliberately thrown away and rebuilt by humans for the features that survive day-90. This dissolves both the maintenance-burden and deskilling problems at once because no AI-authored code ever becomes load-bearing.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist needs the prototype code to convert into validated learning AND remain the shipped artifact to claim the cost savings (throwing it away forfeits the build-cost deflation that funds his whole economic argument). The Skeptic frames the prototype-becoming-production as the inevitable trap rather than a choice, so he never proposes the obvious escape hatch. Both are locked into the premise that 'the same AI-generated prototype' produces either learning or debt — neither questions whether prototype and production code must be the same artifact at all.

arguments.argument: The day-90 kill-or-keep gate optimizes for the wrong variable: for a low-risk consumer feature at an established firm, the dominant cost is rarely catastrophic failure OR maintenance debt — it is the opportunity cost of senior engineering attention diverted to a feature the firm's existing analytics could have predicted would underperform, and which then squats in the roadmap consuming review, on-call, and integration cycles even after it 'survives.' The real Finance question is not 'growth per dollar of build cost' but 'growth per dollar of scarce engineering attention,' a metric the AI-speedup framing systematically obscures because AI cheapens authorship but not the human comprehension, review, and coordination that remain the binding constraint.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist measures cost in build-hours (where AI delivers 26-55% gains) and treats SRE/QA capacity as abundant infrastructure to absorb remediation, so he cannot see attention as the scarce resource. The Skeptic gets close with the deskilling/grader-pool point but frames it as capability erosion over cycles, not as a per-feature attention-allocation problem present from day one. Neither reframes Finance's metric away from cost-per-feature toward cost-per-unit-of-scarce-human-attention, which would reveal that AI's authorship speedup is partially illusory when the binding constraint is comprehension bandwidth that AI does not relieve.

missing_arguments.argument: The debate ignored that for a low-risk consumer feature, the correct strategy is to throw the prototype away on purpose — build it to validate the demand signal, then rewrite the validated 10% as production code, so 'maintenance burden' is a false dilemma you avoid by never promoting prototype code to load-bearing status. Spotlight, Slack, and countless A/B-tested features were validated on disposable scaffolding before any durable engineering investment.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It dissolves the central tug-of-war by denying that prototype code must ever become maintenance burden, which neither side apparently challenged.

missing_arguments.argument: Finance's actual incentive was undersold: growth-per-dollar for an established firm is dominated by the cost of capital and the option value of being first to a learning, not by the marginal maintenance cost of one feature — a feature that captures even a 1% retention lift on an established user base dwarfs a decade of cleanup salary, so Finance should rationally fund speed and pre-budget a refactor reserve rather than treat tech debt as a loss.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It reframes the Finance perspective in real capital-allocation terms (option value, NPV of learning) that the synthesis treated only as a vague 'growth per dollar' tug.

missing_arguments.argument: The biggest hidden cost of AI-generated code at an established company is not maintenance or deskilling but security and supply-chain liability — AI routinely emits plausible-but-vulnerable patterns (hardcoded secrets, injection-prone queries, outdated dependencies), and for a brand with millions of users a single AI-introduced breach converts 'low-risk consumer product' into regulatory exposure, disclosure obligations, and reputational damage that no velocity gain offsets.
missing_arguments.why_strong: Security and breach liability is a concrete, quantifiable operational risk for a large consumer brand that the entire synthesis omitted despite being the most board-visible failure mode.

missing_arguments.argument: The synthesis treated the team as monolithic, but the decisive variable is whether the engineers reviewing AI output have domain context in THIS codebase — AI-generated code reviewed by senior engineers who own the system is validated learning, while the same code shipped by a team using AI to compensate for unfamiliarity converts directly to terminal burden; the conditions for 'help vs. hurt' therefore hinge on reviewer seniority-to-AI-volume ratio, a manageable staffing lever.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It identifies a concrete, controllable operational dial (who reviews, at what ratio) that directly answers the topic's 'under what conditions' question without relying on contested deskilling claims.

missing_arguments.argument: Reversibility, not speed, is the right decision criterion: AI-prototyped MVPs are safe to ship fast precisely when the feature is independently deployable behind a flag and removable in one revert, and dangerous when it requires schema migrations, shared-state changes, or public API contracts that can't be rolled back — so the company should gate AI velocity on architectural reversibility rather than on code-quality virtue.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It supplies a crisp, testable structural gate (reversibility/blast-radius) that is more actionable than the 're-derivability' test the debate centered on and maps cleanly to maintenance-burden containment.
